passage:
Mentor's note, first-year B.Com, Vaibhav
Vaibhav is the most responsible student in my group, and I am starting to worry about that. He is the eldest of four. Since his father's shop closed, he works evening shifts at a courier office and walks his sisters to school every morning. He has never once asked for an extension.
Today he fell asleep during the tutorial. When I asked, he said, 'I'm fine, ma'am, I'm used to it.' Then, very quietly, 'Sometimes I wish I could just go on the college trip like the others.'
What I did next: I told him that wish is normal, not selfish. I connected him with the fee-support office and asked whether an aunt or cousin could share the morning school run. He will ask his mother this weekend. I will check in next Friday.
Ayesha

qa.q: What does Vaibhav do every morning?
qa.a: He walks his sisters to school every morning.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's quiet wish about the college trip reveal?
qa.a: It reveals that behind his sense of duty he is tired and longs for some freedom like the others.

qa.q: What steps did Ayesha take after the tutorial, and why were they wise?
qa.a: She told him the wish is normal, linked him with the fee-support office and suggested sharing the school run, easing his load without shaming his care.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav's sisters be affected if a cousin shares the school run?
qa.a: They would still get to school safely, and might see their brother less exhausted and more like himself.

grounding: Shows an eldest son whose care for family has become his identity, hiding tiredness and a wish for freedom, and a mentor who notices and helps.

passage:
Friday, late
Himani's admission letter came today. Pune! She screamed, Maa cried, and everyone looked at me, because I was the one who sat with her maths every night for two years. I felt proud enough to burst.
Then, while I was closing the dhaba's accounts, a strange heaviness came. I'm twenty-one. I left my own diploma after first year when Papa's back went bad. I cook, I do the accounts, I fix the tap, I take Maa to her check-ups. 'Hemant bhaiya will handle it' is practically our family motto.
I'm not sorry. I love them. But tonight I let myself write it: I want something that's just mine. Maybe a weekend course. Maybe just one day off a week.
Tomorrow I'll tell Maa about the day off. Small start.

qa.q: Where did Himani get admission?
qa.a: Pune.

qa.q: What two feelings does Hemant have on the day of the letter?
qa.a: He feels proud enough to burst about Himani, and later a heavy tiredness about all he carries and a wish for something of his own.

qa.q: What small choice does Hemant plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: To tell Maa he wants one day off a week, a small start toward something that's just his.

qa.q: How might Himani feel if she knew how much her bhaiya carries?
qa.a: Himani may feel grateful and perhaps a little guilty, and might want to support him having his own time.

grounding: Shows an eldest sibling who has delayed his own wants to care for the family, feeling pride along with tiredness and a wish for freedom.

passage: I'm Vikas, twenty-two, the eldest of four, and I don't remember a time I wasn't in charge. When Papa's shop closed, I was sixteen. I started tutoring kids after school so my brothers' fees got paid. I learned to fix the pump, fill in forms, talk to the bank. Everyone says, "Vikas is so responsible, just like his father." My father, Ramesh, pats my back. And I am proud of it. But last month a friend asked me what I want to do, just me, and I couldn't answer. I stood in the shower for ages that night, so tired I couldn't think. I think somewhere I stopped wanting things. I'd like to find out what they were.

qa.q: How old was Vikas when Papa's shop closed?
qa.a: Sixteen.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel when asked about wanting something just for Vikas?
qa.a: Vikas felt lost and very tired, unable to answer because those wants had faded.

qa.q: What could Vikas try next to reconnect with those wishes?
qa.a: Set aside a little time each week just for Vikas, and talk honestly with the family about sharing some duties.

qa.q: How does Ramesh seem to see Vikas?
qa.a: Ramesh seems proud, patting Vikas on the back for being so responsible.

grounding: Shows an eldest child whose caring duty became identity, hiding tiredness and forgotten wishes.

passage:
Monday: Ojas woke at six to pack his three siblings' tiffins, drop them at school, then take his mother, Vasudha, to her hospital appointment before his own college lecture.
Thursday: His friends were leaving on a weekend trek. Ojas said he couldn't; his youngest sister had a test. On the bus home he felt a heaviness he had no name for, and a small, guilty wish to be free for just one day.
The next Sunday: Vasudha found him asleep sitting up on the sofa. "Beta, when did you last do something for yourself?" Ojas laughed, but couldn't answer. She took the siblings' tiffin list off the fridge and wrote her own name on it.

qa.q: How many siblings' tiffins did Ojas pack?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: He felt a nameless heaviness and a guilty wish to be free for one day.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that could ease Ojas's load?
qa.a: She noticed his tiredness, asked about his own life and took over the tiffin list.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel seeing Ojas asleep sitting up?
qa.a: Vasudha probably feels worried and a little guilty about how much he carries.

grounding: Shows over days an eldest child whose duty hides tiredness and a wish for freedom, noticed by a parent.

passage: Dolma, you're the eldest too, so listen. At twenty I ran our house in Shillong. My mother was ill, my father worked in the tea gardens, and I had three younger ones to feed, dress and scold. I stopped my college classes for a year. Everybody called me "the second mother". I, Vidya, was proud of that name. But at night I'd sit on the back steps, too tired to cry, and think about the teachers' training course I'd never applied for. One day my aunt came to stay for a month and said, "Go and fill the form. I'll manage." I did. I didn't stop being the eldest. But I found out there was still a me under all that duty.

qa.q: What did everybody call young Vidya?
qa.a: "The second mother."

qa.q: How did young Vidya feel on the back steps at night?
qa.a: Vidya felt too tired to cry and quietly longed for the training course never applied for.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: The aunt came for a month and told Vidya to fill in the form, making room for Vidya's own wish.

qa.q: How might the aunt have seen Vidya's life?
qa.a: The aunt likely saw a young woman carrying too much and wanted to give her a chance.

grounding: Shows an eldest daughter whose duty became identity, hiding exhaustion and a wish of her own.

passage:
The bus strike began on the same morning as Abbu's clinic appointment and the last day for Kiran's college exam form. Irfan, the eldest, woke at five.
He wheeled Abbu to the auto stand, argued the fare down, sat through the long wait, and got Abbu home by eleven. Then he rode pillion with a neighbour to Kiran's college, stood in line and submitted her form ten minutes before the counter shut.
On the way back, his phone buzzed: his friends' photos from the hill trip he had said no to. He looked for a long time.
At home Ammi asked, "All done?" Irfan said, "All done," and smiled.
Only Kiran saw him lie down on the floor mat without taking off his shoes. She brought him tea. "Bhaiya, next time, give me one of the jobs."

qa.q: How long before the counter shut did Irfan submit Kiran's form?
qa.a: He submitted her form ten minutes before the counter shut.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling as he looked at his friends' trip photos?
qa.a: He felt wistful and tired, quietly wishing for the freedom he had given up to look after the family.

qa.q: What small step could help Irfan carry his duty with less strain?
qa.a: He could accept Kiran's offer and share some of the jobs, instead of hiding his tiredness behind "All done".

qa.q: How does Kiran see her brother that evening?
qa.a: She notices what the others miss, sees how worn out he is, and wants to help carry the load.

grounding: Irfan, the eldest, serves his parents and sister through a hard day, and his duty hides tiredness and a wish for freedom.
